enrichment.short_title: Mother and baby unit exclusion and separation
key_facts: CD, a 19-year-old Jamaican woman serving a three-and-a-half-year sentence for cocaine importation, gave birth to her son AD in the Mother and Baby Unit at Styal prison.

On 19 September 2002 the residential governor excluded CD from the MBU and separated mother and baby after allegations of conflict with other prisoners, without giving her a proper opportunity to answer the allegations.
Joint expert evidence from a consultant psychologist and consultant social worker strongly recommended urgent phased reunification, warning of serious attachment disruption if separation continued.
There were no prescribed Prison Service procedures governing exclusion and separation in these circumstances, despite detailed admission procedures for MBUs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review on behalf of the imprisoned mother and her infant son, represented by the Official Solicitor, of the Prison Service decision to exclude the mother from the MBU and separate her from her baby.
enrichment.outcome: Application for judicial review succeeded; the exclusion and separation decision was quashed and the Prison Service was required to reconsider lawfully.
enrichment.ratio: A decision to exclude a mother from a Mother and Baby Unit and separate her from her baby engages Article 8 and must give primary consideration to the child's best interests, be proportionate after assessing less intrusive alternatives, and be reached only after fair procedures including an opportunity to answer allegations and make representations.
legal_issues: Whether the decision-maker properly considered the child's best interests as the primary consideration
Whether separation was a proportionate and justifiable interference with Article 8 rights
Whether the decision was procedurally fair
Whether a later internal review cured earlier procedural and substantive defects

statutes_considered.title: Transfer of Undertakings (Protection of Employment) Regulations 1981

key_facts: Anthony Marsh successfully claimed unfair dismissal after BLP UK Ltd dismissed him following a customer complaint about late foil deliveries, without following capability procedures or giving warnings.

BLP appealed to the Employment Appeal Tribunal alleging that the employment tribunal chairman had displayed apparent bias through hostile questioning, body language, and markedly different treatment of employer and employee witnesses.
The EAT rejected the bias challenge but remitted compensation issues for lack of reasons.
BLP's further appeal to the Court of Appeal challenged the EAT's application of the objective bias test.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Employer's appeal from the Employment Appeal Tribunal's refusal to set aside an employment tribunal decision on grounds of apparent bias.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the EAT was held to have applied the correct objective test and there was no basis to interfere.
enrichment.ratio: Alleged tribunal bias is assessed by asking whether a fair-minded and informed observer, knowing all relevant circumstances including the chairman's later commentary, would conclude there was a real possibility of bias; strong questioning and less warmth toward a weak employer case do not necessarily satisfy that test.
legal_issues: Whether the EAT applied the correct objective test for apparent bias
Whether the EAT erred in speculating about reasons for differential treatment of witnesses
Whether the EAT improperly relied on impugned tribunal findings of fact
Whether the tribunal chairman's conduct created a real possibility of bias

enrichment.short_title: Employer liability for unauthorised fence climb

statutes_considered.title: Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1992

key_facts: Mr Wallis, an experienced Balfour Beatty track manager, could not open a padlocked access gate while responding to a track caution causing train delays.
Under time pressure he climbed over palisade fencing and a bridge wingwall to reach the line, removed the caution, and fell about 10 to 12 feet on the return route, sustaining a serious back injury.
The recorder found that employee safety was paramount, the improvised route was dangerous and unauthorised, and the accident was not reasonably foreseeable.
The Court of Appeal accepted there was a breach of regulation 17(2) of the Workplace Regulations but held the claimant's own conduct was the sole cause of the accident.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Employee's appeal against dismissal of a personal injury claim at the Central London County Court.
enrichment.ratio: An employer owes a duty to guard against reasonably foreseeable risks, but where safety is treated as paramount and an experienced employee voluntarily chooses a dangerous unauthorised access route that the employer did not expect, the employee's own conduct may break the chain of causation even if a statutory traffic-route breach is established.
legal_issues: Whether the recorder misdirected herself on foreseeability
Whether climbing the fence was a reasonably foreseeable response to a locked access gate
Whether there were breaches of the Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1992
Whether there were breaches of the Workplace (Health, Safety and Welfare) Regulations 1992 and whether any breach caused the accident

enrichment.short_title: Legal aid costs order after dismissed appeals

statutes_considered.title: Community Legal Services Costs Protection Regulations 2000

key_facts: After two related appeals were dismissed, the court was asked to make costs orders against an appellant whose opponent had been funded by the Legal Services Commission.
Brutton & Co sought to preserve their ability to recover appeal costs from the Commission even though underlying proceedings against them might continue.
Concern arose that a section 11 costs order would trigger a three-month time limit for a Regulation 10 application before the outcome of the main action was known.
The court considered whether 'proceedings' for costs purposes meant only the appeal proceedings or the underlying action as a whole.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Post-judgment costs application in the Court of Appeal following dismissal of two appeals in related litigation.
enrichment.outcome: Appellant ordered to pay respondents' costs of each appeal, with detailed assessment and a section 11 referral to a costs judge; liberty to apply reserved for jurisdictional disputes.
enrichment.ratio: For the purposes of a section 11(1) costs order and any subsequent application against the Legal Services Commission, 'proceedings' means the appeal proceedings finally determined in the appellate court, not the continuing underlying action, so a costs judge may later adjourn any premature Commission application until final resolution of the main claim.
legal_issues: Whether a section 11(1) costs order should be made immediately after dismissal of the appeals
Whether the costs judge has jurisdiction to order payment by the Legal Services Commission while underlying proceedings continue
How the three-month Regulation 10 time limit interacts with unresolved main proceedings
The meaning of 'proceedings' in legal aid costs legislation
linked_authorities: General Accident Car and Life Assurance Corporation Ltd v Foster

key_facts: Following the Court of Appeal's judgment of 20 December 2002, the appellant applied for certification of a point of law of general public importance and leave to appeal to the House of Lords.

The certified question concerned whether it is an abuse of process to prosecute indecent assault where the underlying conduct is unlawful sexual intercourse with a girl under 16 in respect of which prosecution is barred.
The court certified the point under section 33(2) of the Criminal Appeal Act 1968.
Leave to appeal to the House of Lords was refused, although a representation order was granted for any further application.

enrichment.outcome: Point of law certified; leave to appeal to the House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: The court may certify as a point of law of general public importance whether prosecuting indecent assault is an abuse of process where the conduct underlying the charge is unlawful sexual intercourse with a girl under 16 that cannot be prosecuted because of the statutory restrictions in the Sexual Offences Act 1956, even if leave to take the point further is refused.

enrichment.short_title: Football kit contract penalty interest clause
key_facts: Jeancharm Ltd, trading as Beaver International, supplied football kit to Barnet Football Club under a 1998 agreement containing reciprocal late-performance clauses.
The contract imposed interest at 5% per week on late invoice payments, equivalent to about 260% per annum, while late delivery attracted 20 pence per garment per day.
After accounting disputes Barnet owed about £5,142, but Jeancharm claimed roughly £20,000 after applying the interest clause.
The judge upheld the clause; the Court of Appeal held it was a penalty and therefore unenforceable.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Supplier's appeal from a circuit judge's decision upholding a contractual late-payment interest clause in a commercial supply agreement.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the 5% per week interest clause was held to be an unenforceable penalty.
enrichment.ratio: A contractual late-payment interest rate is a penalty, not a genuine pre-estimate of loss, when it is extravagant and unconscionable compared with the greatest loss that could conceivably follow from late payment; equal bargaining power does not prevent a clause from being penal if it is plainly deterrent rather than compensatory.
legal_issues: Whether the 5% per week late-payment clause was a penalty or liquidated damages
The correct application of the Dunlop v New Garage tests
Whether reciprocal late-delivery penalties justified the interest clause
Whether the clause could be justified as compensation for administrative costs on a small contract

Phillips Hong Kong Ltd v Attorney General of Hong Kong
Robophone Facilities Ltd v Blank

key_facts: Mr Ahmed was charged with dangerous driving allegedly committed on 2 July 1999, but summonses were repeatedly reissued to an address where he no longer lived and the case lay dormant for long periods.
Despite arrests for other matters and returned-post indications that he was abroad, no effective steps were taken to serve or progress the case until he was arrested on a warrant in January 2002.
A district judge held in May 2002 that there had been no breach of the right to trial within a reasonable time, analysing delay in segmented periods rather than as a whole.
By the anticipated trial date in 2002, about three years had elapsed in a straightforward summary offence case.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a magistrates' court ruling that the defendant's Article 6 right to trial within a reasonable time had not been breached.
enrichment.outcome: Decision quashed; the case was not remitted to the magistrates' court because of the further delay that remittal would cause.
enrichment.ratio: In assessing whether a criminal charge has been tried within a reasonable time under Article 6, the court must consider the overall delay from charge to anticipated trial and cannot treat periods separately so as to absolve the prosecution where cumulative delay in a simple case is unusually long, even if the defendant is not personally at fault for service failures.
legal_issues: Whether the overall delay from July 1999 to anticipated trial in 2002 breached Article 6
Whether the district judge erred by dividing the delay into separate periods
Whether prosecution, police, or court inactivity caused the delay
Whether the matter should be remitted for reconsideration

confidence.notes: Chronology, Article 6 reasoning, and relief are clearly explained. The judgment relies on factual documents not all present in the source file.

enrichment.short_title: Small claim defence struck out over expert letter
key_facts: Mr Yorke claimed £2,789.63 for building work in a small claim allocated to the small claims track.
District Judge Enzer ordered a joint expert on workmanship and directed that unless Mr Katra signed the agreed letter of instruction by 17 October 2001 his defence would be struck out.
Mr Katra signed the letter but struck out two sentences he considered inaccurate, whereupon the district judge struck out his defence and entered judgment.
Further applications were dismissed by District Judge Raeside and Judge Hull QC; Judge Harris held he had no jurisdiction to hear an appeal against Judge Hull's procedural order.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Defendant's application for permission to appeal and extension of time against county court orders striking out his defence in a small building claim.
enrichment.outcome: Application allowed in part; the court reconstituted itself in the High Court and indicated the appeal against Judge Hull's order was strongly arguable, with directions for consent resolution or an oral appeal.
enrichment.ratio: Where a litigant in person in a small building claim signs a joint expert letter of instruction in substantially usable form but deletes non-essential sentences, striking out the defence for non-compliance may be an unjust technical forfeiture of a merits hearing, and an appellate court may treat the matter as an appeal against the earlier procedural refusal rather than as an appeal with no jurisdiction.
legal_issues: Whether Judge Harris had jurisdiction to hear the application
Whether Judge Hull should have treated the application as permission to appeal the district judges' strike-out orders
Whether strike-out was justified where the defendant signed the expert letter with minor deletions
The appropriate route to challenge Judge Hull's procedural order

confidence.notes: Procedural history and Dyson LJ's reasoning are clear, though the judgment is an interlocutory permission decision rather than a final merits ruling.

enrichment.short_title: Clinical negligence costs hourly rates appeal
key_facts: The claimant recovered £3.5 million plus capped education costs in a severe birth brain injury clinical negligence claim shortly before trial.
Liability was admitted only ten working days before trial, after which a Part 36 offer was accepted on 27 April 2001.
On detailed assessment the costs judge allowed a partner hourly rate of £300 and leading counsel at £350, finding the case heavy, complex, and expertly run.
The defendant health authority appealed on the partner rate, delegation, and counsel's hourly rate.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with assessors from a costs judge's detailed assessment decisions in a high-value clinical negligence claim.
enrichment.ratio: On appeal from a costs judge, the court will not interfere with an hourly rate or delegation decision unless it was wrong; exceptionally heavy and complex clinical negligence litigation may justify high partner and silk rates where the costs judge, using his expertise, concludes they were reasonably incurred and proportionate, without treating those figures as a general norm.
legal_issues: Whether £300 per hour for the partner was a reasonable and proportionate rate
Whether the partner failed to delegate work appropriately
Whether £350 per hour for leading counsel was reasonable
The proper use of A plus B analysis and guideline rates on detailed assessment

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (Environmental Impact Assessment) (England and Wales) Regulations 1999

key_facts: Mr Payne applied under Schedule 13 paragraph 9 of the Environment Act 1995 for the council to determine conditions for two old mineral permissions relating to colliery waste tipping and tip removal at Senghenydd.
The council rejected the application in relation to the 1961 permission because its time-limited consent had expired, and declined to treat the 1955 permission application as valid.
The High Court held the 1955 application was valid and, because the council gave no decision within three months, the proposed conditions were deemed determined under paragraph 9(9).
The council appealed, arguing the proposed conditions were outside the scope of the permission and that environmental impact assessment regulations disapplied the deemed-determination mechanism.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Council's appeal and landowner's cross-application for permission to appeal from a High Court judicial review decision on a Schedule 13 paragraph 9 ROMP application.
enrichment.outcome: Council's appeal dismissed in relation to the 1955 permission; Mr Payne's application for permission to appeal concerning the lapsed 1961 permission refused.
enrichment.ratio: A paragraph 9 application to determine conditions for a dormant mineral permission is valid unless proposed conditions would fundamentally change the permission's nature; where a valid application receives no decision within three months the conditions specified in the application are deemed determined, and that mechanism is not disapplied merely because tipping colliery waste is not EIA Schedule 2 underground mining or waste-installation development.
legal_issues: Whether the application validly identified the mineral site and proposed permissible conditions
Whether proposed conditions for the 1955 permission were so exorbitant as to invalidate the application
Whether EIA regulations disapplied paragraph 9(9) deemed determination
Whether paragraph 9 applies to a mineral permission that is no longer extant, such as the 1961 permission
linked_authorities: R v North Lincolnshire County Council ex parte Horticultural and Garden Products Sales (Humberside) Ltd

confidence.notes: Statutory framework, validity analysis, EIA argument, and lapsed-permission conclusion are clearly reasoned in the judgment.
